newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Netanyahu and bitter Arafat to meet Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu and bitter Arafat to meet Thursday.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian leaders, at what they called positive and productive talks in Switzerland, agreed on Sunday to meet again on Thursday for detailed talks on extending Palestinian self-rule.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said this reflected "a great feeling of hope" and he was confident that he and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat could overcome the obstacles to Middle East peace.

But, in a bitter speech to an audience of prominent business and political leaders, Arafat later complained that Israel was violating the peace agreements, dragging its feet on putting them into practice and stifling the Palestinian economy.

"Is this a just peace? Is this the peace expected by the world? Our nation is the only one paying a price for peace. Our nation is paying a harsh price," he told the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, also in the Swiss resort of Davos, said new peace talks between Israel and Syria were inevitable and could take place at any time.

Mubarak was speaking after a meeting with Netanyahu, their first for more than six months. He had refused to meet the Israeli leader until he reached agreement with the Palestinians on the West bank town of Hebron.
Netanyahu and Arafat clinched a Hebron deal last month but after an initial period of optimism the Palestinians are again complaining about Israeli policies and practices.
"We have kept up our side of the agreement and exerted all possible efforts to resume the negotiations with the new Israeli government to implement the interim agreement," Arafat said.
"The problem we face today is the procrastination with which Israel is implementing its part of its agreement and the failure to solve several pending problems."

He said Israel was still confiscating Arab land and building Jewish settlements. He also said Israeli restrictions on the movement of people and goods between Israel and the Palestinian territories were costing Palestinians $7 million a day.
Arafat later told a news conference that the Israel's motives were to inflict collective punishment and exert political pressure on the Palestinians.
Netanyahu told his news conference that his government had in fact eased the closure of the Palestinian territories and sincerely wanted the Palestinians to prosper.

The immediate Palestinian demands include the release of prisoners, a safe passage between Gaza and the West Bank, fewer restrictions on the flow of people and goods and clearance for Gaza airport to open and work to start on a Gaza seaport.

Netanyahu said: "Chairman Arafat and I have just a very productive meeting...We are going to meet again to discuss specific implementation steps by Israel and the Palestinians on the agreement that we have reached following Hebron.

"I think this reflects a new attitude, maybe a new beginnning. There's certainly a great feeling of hope...and I'm confident as a result of today's meetings and for other reasons as well that we will overcome the obstacles."
On the prospects for talks with Syria, frozen for almost a year, Netanyahu said the United States was seeking a formula for negotiations to resume.
"We're discussing the formula... he Americans are doing this and I hope they'll be successful," he said.

"I cannot force President (Hafez) al-Assad to resume the peace talks. If he wants to, we'll find the formula. If he doesn't want to, there can always be 100 reasons given why we cannot start the peace talks."

Mubarak, asked about the chances for Syrian-Israeli talks, said: "I believe Syria says it's ready to start the talks, even if it may have some reservations. But this is a question of time and it's bound to be resolved."
Mubarak earlier linked progress on the Syrian-Israeli track to faithful Israeli implementation of its latest agreements with the Palestinians, including the deal on Hebron.

But Syria has not taken the Hebron agreement as a sign of a change of heart by Netanyahu's rightwing government. Damascus says talks must resume where they left off and Israel has given a private commitment to withdraw from all of the Golan Heights.
